title: DNA and RNA: the instructions inside every living thing

summary.text: Grow moong, methi and mustard seeds side by side on the same wet cotton, and each grows their own shape of leaf. The shape comes from inside the seed. Every living thing carries instructions for building their body. These instructions are written in a long, thin molecule called DNA, using just four chemical letters: A, T, C and G. A cell copies the part they need into a shorter molecule called RNA, and uses that copy to build proteins, the parts that do the body's work. You got half of your DNA from your mother and half from your father.
summary.art: Three rows of tiny seedlings on wet cotton in a steel plate by a window: moong with fat seed halves, methi with small oval leaves, mustard with notched heart-shaped leaves. Above them, a faint twisted ladder of DNA with the letters A, T, C and G on its rungs.

intro.hook: Take three seeds from the kitchen: a moong bean, a methi seed and a mustard seed. Put them on the same wet cotton, by the same window, with the same water. Will they grow into the same kind of plant? If not, where does each plant's shape come from?
intro.text: The cotton, water and light give a seedling the materials and energy to grow. But they give every seed the same things. So the difference must be inside each seed. In this unit you grow the seeds and see. Then you find out what is inside: a set of instructions called DNA. Every cell of every living thing carries them, including every cell of you.
intro.art: A child's palm holding a green moong bean, a yellow-brown methi seed and a tiny dark mustard seed, next to a steel plate with wet cotton.

outcomes: I can explain that every living thing carries instructions, called DNA, that shape their body.
I can run a fair test with three kinds of seed grown in the same place, and say what my results show.
I can say that DNA is written in four chemical letters, A, T, C and G, and that the order of the letters carries the instructions.
I can explain how a cell uses RNA: the cell copies one gene from the DNA into RNA, and uses the copy to build a protein.
I can explain why a child looks a little like each parent: half of their DNA comes from each.
I can tell how scientists found out that DNA, not protein, carries the instructions.

terms.meaning: DNA is a very long, thin molecule inside cells. It holds the instructions for building and running a living body. A molecule is a group of atoms joined together.
terms.example: The DNA in a methi seed holds the instructions for methi leaves that come in threes.
terms.art: A twisted ladder with coloured rungs, coming out of a cell drawn as a round room.

terms.meaning: A gene is one stretch of DNA that holds the instructions for one job, usually for building one protein. Your DNA holds about 20,000 genes.
terms.example: One gene holds the instructions for keratin, the protein your hair and nails are made of.
terms.art: A long ribbon of letters with one short stretch of it coloured in.

terms.meaning: RNA is a molecule a cell makes as a copy of one gene. The DNA stays safe in its place, and the RNA copy is carried away and used. RNA uses the letter U in place of T.
terms.example: Like copying one recipe from a big cookbook onto a slip of paper, and taking only the slip to the kitchen.
terms.art: A big closed book on a shelf and a small paper slip with a few lines copied from it.

terms.meaning: A protein is a molecule that a cell builds by joining smaller parts called amino acids in a chain. Proteins do most of the work in a body: they build, carry, digest and protect.
terms.example: A protein in your spit begins to break down rice into sugar. Chew plain rice for a minute, and it starts to taste a little sweet.
terms.art: A chain of beads folding up into a small knotted shape.

terms.meaning: A cell is the smallest living part of a body. Most cells are far too small to see without a microscope. Your body is made of many millions of millions of cells.
terms.example: The thin skin inside an onion is one layer of cells, which you can see with a microscope.
terms.art: A round cell with a darker round nucleus inside it.

terms.meaning: The nucleus is the part of a cell where the DNA is kept. It is usually a round shape near the middle of the cell.
terms.example: In one of your cells, about 2 metres of DNA is folded up inside a nucleus smaller than a hundredth of a millimetre.
terms.art: A cell cut open to show a round nucleus with a tangle of thread inside.

terms.meaning: To inherit is to get something from your parents. Living things inherit DNA from their parents, and with it the instructions for many features.
terms.example: Meena inherited half her DNA from her mother and half from her father, so she looks a little like each of them.
terms.art: A mother, a father and a child, with a thin line of DNA running from each parent to the child.

terms.meaning: A chromosome is one long piece of DNA, wound up tightly so that it fits in the nucleus. Most of your cells have 46 chromosomes: 23 from your mother and 23 from your father.
terms.example: A mustard plant's DNA and a person's DNA are both kept in chromosomes, but different numbers of them.
terms.art: Pairs of X-shaped chromosomes laid out in a row, like socks in pairs.

terms.meaning: A seed leaf is one of the first leaves a seedling opens. It was already folded up inside the seed. Its shape is often different from the plant's later leaves.
terms.example: A mustard seedling opens two seed leaves shaped like small hearts with a notch at the top.
terms.art: A mustard seedling with two notched heart-shaped seed leaves on a thin white stem.

explanations.definition: Every living thing builds their body by following instructions stored inside their cells. These instructions are written in a molecule called DNA.
explanations.description: Water, air, light and food give a living thing the materials and energy to grow. They do not set the shape. A moong seed and a mustard seed on the same wet cotton get exactly the same water and light, yet each grows their own kind of leaf. The difference is in the instructions each seed carries. A seed packs a complete set of DNA in every one of their cells. So do you, and so does an ant, a mango tree and the bacteria in curd.
examples: A tamarind seed grows into a tamarind tree, never into a coconut palm, even in the same soil.
Curd bacteria added to milk make more curd bacteria, not some other kind.
A hen's egg hatches into a chick, and a crow's egg into a crow.
explanations.art: A moong seedling, a methi seedling and a mustard seedling side by side on cotton, each with a tiny scroll of instructions drawn inside their seed.
explanations.context: This card says where a living thing's shape comes from. It is the idea behind the three-seed test.

explanations.concept: Four letters, in a very long line
explanations.definition: DNA is a chain of four kinds of small chemical parts. Scientists name them by the letters A, T, C and G. The order of these letters along the chain holds the instructions.
explanations.description: DNA looks like a long ladder twisted round and round. Each rung of the ladder is a pair of letters. A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G. With only four letters, the order is what matters, just as the same letters make different words: 'pat' and 'tap'. One set of your DNA has about 3 billion letter pairs. Reading one letter every second, without ever stopping, would take nearly 100 years. Every known living thing with cells uses the same four letters.
examples: ATG and GTA use the same three letters but say different things to a cell.
A mustard plant and you both use A, T, C and G. Only the order and the length differ.
Stretched out, the DNA in one of your cells would be about 2 metres long.
explanations.art: A twisted ladder in which each rung is two coloured blocks, labelled A with T and C with G.
explanations.context: This card says what DNA is made of, and why only four letters are enough.

explanations.definition: A gene is a stretch of DNA that holds the instructions for one protein. A protein is a chain of smaller parts called amino acids, folded into a shape that does a job.
explanations.description: Proteins do most of the work in a living body. Keratin builds your hair and nails. Haemoglobin, in your blood, carries oxygen. A protein in your spit breaks starch into sugar. Each protein is made of up to 20 kinds of amino acid joined in a chain. The gene says which amino acids go in which order. The order decides how the chain folds, and the fold decides the job.
examples: Chew plain rice for a minute, and the protein in your spit starts turning its starch into a sugar that tastes sweet.
Keratin, a protein, makes hair, nails, a bird's feathers and a cow's horns.
A green leaf is green because of chlorophyll, which the leaf's proteins build.
explanations.art: A strip of DNA letters with an arrow to a chain of beads folding into a knot, and that knot holding a red blood cell's oxygen.
explanations.context: This card says what the instructions in DNA are for: building proteins, the parts that do a body's work.

explanations.definition: RNA is a copy of one gene, made by the cell. The DNA stays in the nucleus, and the RNA copy is carried out to be read.
explanations.description: Think of DNA as a big family cookbook that never leaves the shelf. When the cell needs a protein, they copy just that one recipe, the gene, into RNA. RNA uses the letter U in place of T, but otherwise it says the same thing. The RNA copy travels out of the nucleus to a ribosome. A ribosome is a tiny part of the cell that builds proteins. It reads the RNA three letters at a time, and each group of three tells it which amino acid to add next. RNA copies are used and then broken down, so the cell makes new ones when needed. Venki Ramakrishnan, born in Chidambaram in Tamil Nadu, shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2009 for working out the structure of the ribosome.
examples: DNA in the nucleus is like the cookbook on the shelf. RNA is the slip with one recipe copied out.
A ribosome reading RNA is like a cook following the slip to make one dish.
The flu virus and the virus that causes COVID-19 keep their own genes in RNA, not DNA.
explanations.art: A cell: in the nucleus, a long DNA ladder with one short stretch being copied onto a single strand of RNA, which then travels out to a small round ribosome that is joining beads into a chain.
explanations.context: This card explains what RNA does: it carries a copy of one gene from the DNA to where proteins are built.

explanations.definition: Almost every cell in a body has the same complete DNA. Each kind of cell uses a different set of its genes.
explanations.description: A cell in a mustard leaf and a cell in their root carry the same DNA. The leaf cell uses the genes for making chlorophyll and catching light. The root cell uses genes for soaking up water. In your body, a skin cell, a muscle cell and a nerve cell also share one DNA, and read different parts. Your red blood cells are an exception: as they grow, they lose their nucleus, so they carry no DNA at all.
examples: Your eye cells and your toe cells have the same DNA, but use different genes.
A methi seedling's seed leaves turn green only in the light, because light leads their cells to make chlorophyll.
Moong sprouts grown in the dark stay pale yellow, because their cells need light to finish making chlorophyll.
explanations.art: One open book with the same pages, and three readers: a leaf cell reading the green page, a root cell reading the water page and a flower cell reading the yellow page.
explanations.context: This card explains how cells with the same DNA can become different parts of one body.

explanations.definition: A child inherits half of their DNA from their mother and half from their father. A plant's seed gets half from the egg in the flower and half from the pollen.
explanations.description: Most of your cells hold two sets of DNA, one from each parent. Each parent passes on a different mix of their own genes in every egg or sperm. That is why brothers and sisters look alike in some ways and different in others. Identical twins grow from one fertilised egg that split in two, so they share the same DNA. Even they are not exactly the same, because they grow in slightly different ways.
examples: Lakshmi has her mother's curly hair and her father's wide smile.
Two sisters from the same parents can have different eye shapes, because each got a different mix.
Kittens born to one mother cat at the same time can have different colours of fur.
explanations.art: A family tree of three generations, with coloured threads from each grandparent running down and mixing in the child at the bottom.
explanations.context: This card explains why you look a little like each of your parents.

explanations.concept: Instructions or surroundings: which shapes a living thing more?
explanations.description: Scientists agree that both DNA and surroundings shape every living thing. The same moong seeds grow short and green in light, and tall and pale in the dark. People with the same DNA, identical twins, still grow up different. What scientists argue about is how much each one matters, and the answer is different for every feature.
examples: Moong seeds from one packet grow differently in light and dark.
Your height depends on your DNA and also on the food you ate as you grew.
Identical twins have different fingerprints.

perspectives.explanation: For many features, such as eye colour or blood group, DNA decides almost everything. Surroundings change only small details.
DNA and surroundings work together at every step. A gene does nothing until the cell uses it, and what the cell senses around them decides when and how.

explanations.art: A scale balance with a DNA ladder on one side and a sun, a water drop and a bowl of food on the other.
explanations.context: This card is about a real argument: how much of a living thing comes from their DNA, and how much from where they grow.

explanations.concept: How a cell decides which genes to use
explanations.description: A cell senses light, warmth, food and signals from neighbouring cells, and switches genes on and off in answer. A methi seedling's cells sense the light and begin making chlorophyll. Cells in your skin sense the sun and make more of a dark colour called melanin, which shields the skin. Scientists know many of the molecules that do the switching. How all these choices fit together inside one cell is still being worked out.
examples: After days in the sun, cells in your skin make more melanin, and the skin grows darker.
A seedling's cells sense light and begin making chlorophyll within hours.
When you cut your finger, cells near the cut switch on genes for healing.

perspectives.who: Biologists who study cells as decision-makers
perspectives.explanation: A cell senses, weighs signals and chooses what to do, much as any living being does. Reading their DNA is part of how they act.
The switching is a chain of chemical reactions. Calling it a choice is a useful way of describing it.

explanations.art: A cell with small sensors on their skin catching sunlight, with a switch inside the nucleus turning on a short stretch of DNA.
explanations.context: This card is about what is still being found out: how a cell chooses which of their genes to use.

agreed.text: In every living thing made of cells, the instructions passed from parents to young are stored in DNA.
agreed.evidence: Experiments in the 1940s and 1950s showed that DNA alone could pass on features in bacteria and viruses. Since then, the DNA of thousands of kinds of living things has been read letter by letter.

agreed.text: All known living things with cells use the same four DNA letters, and almost the same code for turning them into proteins.
agreed.evidence: A human gene put into bacteria is read correctly. Since the 1980s, bacteria carrying the human gene for insulin have made insulin for people with diabetes.

agreed.text: A cell copies a gene into RNA, and a ribosome reads the RNA to build a protein.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have watched this happen in cells, and have photographed ribosomes at the size of single atoms.

agreed.text: A child gets half of their DNA from each parent.
agreed.evidence: Reading the DNA of parents and children shows that each child's two sets match one set from the mother and one from the father.

challenging.claim: Proteins, not DNA, carry the instructions.
challenging.for: Proteins are made of 20 kinds of amino acids, so they seemed able to hold far more instructions than DNA, with its four letters.
challenging.against: Experiments with bacteria in 1944 and with viruses in 1952 showed that DNA, not protein, passes the instructions on. Four letters are enough, because the chain is so long.
challenging.context: This card is about an idea most scientists once held, and how it was shown wrong.

challenging.claim: Features pass from parents to children through the blood.
challenging.who: An old idea in many countries, still heard in sayings such as 'it runs in the blood'
challenging.for: Children do look like their parents, and blood seemed like the part of the body that joins a family.
challenging.against: Features pass on through the DNA in the egg and the sperm. Your red blood cells have no DNA at all. People who receive blood from someone else do not take on that person's looks.
challenging.context: This card is about a common saying, and what really passes from parents to children.

challenging.claim: Your DNA decides everything about you.
challenging.who: A common idea, often heard in news stories about 'a gene for' something
challenging.for: DNA really does decide many features, such as blood group and much of eye colour.
challenging.against: Surroundings shape living things too. Moong seeds from one packet grow tall and pale in the dark and short and green in the light. Identical twins have different fingerprints.
challenging.context: This card is about how much DNA decides, and what else matters.

challenging.claim: Every living thing keeps their instructions in DNA.
challenging.for: Everything made of cells does keep their instructions in DNA.
challenging.against: Many viruses, such as the flu virus and the virus that causes COVID-19, keep their genes in RNA instead. Whether a virus counts as a living thing is itself an open question.
challenging.context: This card is about viruses, which break a rule most books give.

challenging.claim: Life began with RNA, before there was any DNA.
challenging.who: Many scientists who study how life began
challenging.for: RNA can carry instructions like DNA, and some RNA can also do jobs like a protein. So RNA alone could have done both jobs at the start.
challenging.against: Nobody has yet made RNA that copies itself fully, and other scientists think life may have begun in other ways.
challenging.context: This card is about a leading idea for how life began, which is still being tested.

big_questions.q: Every cell in your body has the same DNA. So how does one cell know to become skin, and another to become bone?
big_questions.hint: Think of the cookbook. Does every cook in a big kitchen make every dish?

big_questions.q: If DNA is a set of instructions, who or what reads them?
big_questions.hint: A ribosome reads RNA. Is the ribosome the reader, or the whole cell, or the whole living being?

big_questions.q: A tiny mustard seed carries the plan for a whole mustard plant. Is the plan the same thing as the plant?
big_questions.hint: Could you grow a mustard plant from the plan alone, without water, air and light?

big_questions.q: Every living thing with cells uses the same four letters. What might that tell us about where all living things came from?
big_questions.hint: Families who share a recipe often learned it from the same grandmother.

big_questions.q: Your DNA came from your parents, and theirs from their parents. How far back does your DNA go?
big_questions.hint: Your DNA has been copied, without a break, from parent to child since long before there were people.

story.title: The Spilled Seeds
story.note: The people and events are made up. The science is real: moong, methi and mustard seeds sprout on wet cotton in a few days, and their seed leaves look different from each other.
text: Kavya lived with her mother, her little brother Arjun and her Paati in a flat in Madurai. Paati means grandmother in Tamil. Kavya was nine, and Arjun was six.

Paati had a cookbook. It was not a printed book. It was an old notebook with a brown cover, filled with recipes in Paati's neat Tamil writing. Some pages were from Paati's own mother. Paati kept it locked in the steel almirah, wrapped in a cloth.
One evening Arjun wanted to make neer mor, the cool spiced buttermilk Paati made in summer. 'Bring me the book,' he said. 'I'll cook from it.'
'The book never comes into the kitchen,' said Paati. 'Oil splashes. Water spills. If one page is ruined, that recipe is gone for ever.'

So Kavya opened the almirah, unwrapped the book and found the page. She copied the recipe onto a slip of paper, word by word. One cup of curd. Three cups of water. A pinch of salt. Curry leaves, ginger and one green chilli, crushed. Then she put the book back, and took only the slip to the kitchen.
Arjun made the neer mor, reading from the slip. It tasted just like Paati's. The slip got wet, so they threw it away. The book stayed safe in the almirah.

That week Kavya was doing a science test. On a steel plate she laid wet cotton. In one row she put five green moong beans. In the next row, five yellow-brown methi seeds. In the last row, five tiny black mustard seeds. She put the plate on the window ledge in the hall.
'Don't touch it,' she told Arjun. 'Every seed gets the same water and the same light. Only the seed is different.'

On the second morning, Arjun wanted to help. He carried the plate to the tap to water it. The plate tipped. The seeds slid off the cotton into the sink. Arjun quickly picked them up and pushed them back onto the cotton, anywhere. By the time Kavya came, the rows were gone. The seeds were all mixed up.
Kavya looked at the plate. Some seeds had already split open, with tiny white roots poking out. 'Now I won't know which is which,' she said.
Arjun's eyes filled with tears. Paati came to look. She put on her glasses and peered at the plate for a long time.
'Wait two days,' Paati said. 'Then we'll see.'
Every morning Kavya dripped water onto the cotton with a spoon. The roots grew longer. Pale stems pushed up and stood straight. On the fourth day, each little stem opened two small leaves.
Kavya and Arjun bent over the plate with Paati's magnifying glass.
Some seedlings had a thick stem, with the two fat halves of a bean on top, and two pointed leaves peeping out between them. 'Moong,' said Kavya.
Some had two small, smooth, oval leaves, pale green. 'Methi,' said Paati. 'I have grown methi on this ledge for forty years.'
And some had two tiny leaves shaped like hearts, each with a little notch at the top. 'Mustard!' said Arjun. He pointed at each one.
They counted. Five moong, five methi, five mustard, all mixed up together on the same cotton. Not one had got muddled.
'How did they know?' asked Arjun. 'I put them in the wrong places.'
Kavya thought about it. 'The place didn't matter,' she said slowly. 'They all had the same water and the same light. So the shape must come from inside each seed.'

That evening Kavya read about it in her science book, and then she explained it to Arjun. 'Inside every seed there are instructions. They are written in a long, thin molecule called DNA. A mustard seed's DNA has the instructions for mustard leaves. A methi seed's DNA has the instructions for methi leaves.'
'Like Paati's cookbook,' said Arjun.

'Just like it,' said Kavya. 'The DNA stays safe inside a part of each cell, like the book in the almirah. When a cell needs to build something, they copy one small part of it. That copy is called RNA. It is like my slip of paper. The cell uses the copy and then throws it away. The DNA stays safe.'
Arjun looked at the seedlings. 'So every seed carries their own cookbook,' he said. 'Even the tiny mustard ones.'
'Every cell carries one,' said Kavya. 'In the seedlings, in Paati, in you.'
Paati laughed. 'And where did my cookbook come from?' she asked. 'From my mother, and hers before her. Half of your DNA came from your Amma, and half from your Appa. And some of it came from me.'
Arjun held out his hand and looked at it for a long time.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the seeds were mixed up by accident, but each still grew their own kind of seed leaf. All fifteen had the same cotton, water and light, so the shapes could only come from inside the seeds. Kavya's cookbook and slip match the real science: DNA stays in the nucleus of each cell, like the book in the almirah, and a cell copies one gene into RNA, like the recipe on the slip. The copy is used and then broken down, while the DNA is kept. Paati's last line is true too: half of a child's DNA comes from each parent, and a quarter, roughly, from each grandparent.
ask: Why did Paati say to wait two days before trying to sort the seeds?
All fifteen seeds were mixed up on the same cotton. How could Kavya still tell which was which?
Why did Kavya copy the recipe onto a slip, instead of taking the book to the kitchen? What in a cell is like the book, and what is like the slip?
Arjun said every seed carries their own cookbook. Where in your body is your cookbook kept?
Paati's cookbook had pages from her own mother. What in you came from your grandparents?

games.title: Creature Code: build a creature from four letters
games.context: In this drawing game, each player gets a four-letter code and draws the creature it describes. Players with the same code compare their creatures.

printables.title: 1 key card for each player
items: THE KEY. Letter 1 is the body: A round, T long, C square, G triangle. Letter 2 is the legs: A two, T four, C six, G no legs. Letter 3 is the eyes: A one, T two, C three, G five. Letter 4 is something extra: A wings, T a tail, C horns, G spots.

rules: Shuffle the code cards and put them face down.
Each player takes one code card and keeps it secret.
Everyone uses the key to draw their creature, one letter at a time.
When all have finished, show the creatures. Can the others guess your code from your creature?
Two cards say ATCG and two say TACG. If two players had the same code, put their creatures side by side. What is the same, and what is different?
Play again with new cards. Playing alone, draw three creatures and then decode them the next day.

setup.art: A key card and a code card reading ATCG on a table, a child drawing a round creature with four legs and three eyes.
setup.caption: 1. Take a code card. Use the key to draw.

setup.art: Two drawings of the same round, four-legged, three-eyed, spotted creature, drawn in slightly different styles.
setup.caption: 2. Same code? Compare your creatures.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the key and the code cards. 2. Give each player a key, paper and a pencil. 3. Shuffle the code cards.
flow.say: Each code card has four letters, like a tiny piece of DNA. Each letter gives one instruction. Let's see what creature your code builds.
flow.kid: Take a code card. Keep it secret. Each letter tells you one part to draw.

flow.do: Everyone draws their creature from their code, letter by letter.
flow.say: Draw the body first, from letter 1. Then the legs from letter 2, the eyes from letter 3 and the extra from letter 4.
flow.kid: Letter 1 is the body. Letter 2 is legs. Letter 3 is eyes. Letter 4 is the extra. Draw!

flow.do: Show the creatures. Guess each other's codes. Put any matching codes side by side.
flow.say: Two creatures from the same code. Are they the same? What is different about them?
flow.kid: Look at two creatures from one code. What is the same? What is different?

check.q: Two players both drew from the code ATCG. Both creatures are round, with four legs, three eyes and spots. But one is drawn bigger and in green. Why?
options: The code set the parts, and each player's drawing added their own details
check.why: The same code gave the same parts every time: round body, four legs, three eyes, spots. Size and colour were not in the code, so they came from who drew it and how. Living things are like this too: DNA sets the plan, and where and how a body grows changes the details. Picking 'the code was different' forgets that both cards said ATCG.

games.title: Seed and Plant Pairs: a memory game
games.context: In this memory game you match each seed card with the plant that grows from that seed. Every seed carries the instructions for their own kind of plant.

printables.title: 24 cards to cut out: 12 seeds and 12 plants
items: SEED: a tiny round mustard seed
PLANT: mustard, with yellow flowers and thin pods
PLANT: methi, with small leaves in threes
PLANT: moong, with long thin hairy pods
SEED: a brown, shiny tamarind seed
PLANT: a tall tamarind tree, with tiny leaflets and curved brown pods
PLANT: a coconut palm, with long feathery leaves
SEED: a big flat mango stone
PLANT: a mango tree, with long dark green leaves
PLANT: a jackfruit tree, with huge spiky fruits on the trunk
SEED: a tiny flat tomato seed
PLANT: a tomato plant, with yellow flowers and red fruits

rules: Shuffle the 24 cards and lay them face down in a grid.
On your turn, turn over two cards.
If they are a seed and the plant that grows from that seed, keep the pair and say one thing the seed's instructions build. Then take another turn.
If not, turn them face down again.
The player with the most pairs at the end wins. Playing alone, count how many turns you need, and try to beat it next time.

flow.do: Cut out and shuffle the 24 cards. Lay them face down in a grid.
flow.say: Every seed carries the instructions for one kind of plant. Can you find each seed's plant?
flow.kid: Lay all the cards face down. Find each seed and the plant they grow into.

flow.do: Take turns turning over two cards, as in the rules.
flow.say: When you find a pair, tell us one thing that seed's instructions build. A flower? A pod? A trunk?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. A pair? Say one thing that seed will build.

flow.say: A mango stone and a mustard seed both fall on the same soil. Why do they grow so differently?

check.q: A mango stone and a mustard seed fall on the same soil and get the same rain. Why does one grow into a tree and the other into a small plant?
options: Each seed carries their own instructions, in their DNA
The rain is different for each seed
check.why: The soil and rain are the same for both seeds. The difference is the DNA each seed carries, with the instructions for their own kind of plant. Picking 'the soil chooses' is a common idea, but a mango stone never grows mustard, whatever soil it lands in.

experiments.title: Three Seeds, One Cotton: where does a plant's shape come from?
experiments.question: If moong, methi and mustard seeds grow on the same wet cotton, with the same water and light, will their seedlings look the same?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the three kinds of seedling look the same, or different? Which kind will sprout first? Which will be tallest on day 4? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All the seeds lie on the same cotton, on one plate, in one place, and get the same water. Only the kind of seed changes. We use five seeds of each kind, because one seed might be old or damaged.
results_table: Height of the tallest on day 4 (cm)

materials.item: 5 whole green moong beans
5 methi seeds
5 mustard seeds, black or brown, from the kitchen
a steel plate or a plastic lid
cotton wool, or 4 layers of tissue paper or old cotton cloth
a spoon and a cup of water
3 small paper labels and a pencil
a ruler
a magnifying glass, if you have one

schedule.what: Guess. Lay out three rows of seeds on wet cotton. Put the plate by a window.
Add a spoon or two of water. Write down which seeds show a root.
Add water. Look for stems standing up.
Look closely, measure and draw the seed leaves. Compare the three kinds. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw one seedling of each kind on day 4, as big as you can, showing the shape of the two seed leaves.
experiments.context: In this experiment you grow three kinds of kitchen seed side by side on the same wet cotton, and see whether they grow alike.

setup.art: A steel plate with a layer of wet cotton, and three rows of seeds on it: green moong, yellow-brown methi and tiny dark mustard, each row with a paper label.
setup.caption: 1. Lay 5 seeds of each kind in three rows on wet cotton.

setup.art: The plate on a window ledge in bright light but not in hot afternoon sun, a spoon dripping water onto the cotton.
setup.caption: 2. Keep it by a window. Add a spoon of water each day.

setup.art: A child with a magnifying glass looking at three rows of seedlings on day 4, a ruler beside the plate.
setup.caption: 3. On day 4, measure the seedlings and draw their seed leaves.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Two fat bean halves, with two small pointed leaves between them
Two tiny heart-shaped leaves with a notch at the top

flow.do: 1. Put one seed of each kind on your child's palm. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason before anything else.
flow.say: These three seeds will get the same cotton, the same water and the same light. Will they grow into seedlings that look the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the three seeds. They will get the same water and light. Will they grow the same? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Will the seedlings look the same or different? Why?
good: Different, because they are different kinds of seed.
The same, because they get the same things.
Any guess with a reason is a good start.

flow.parent: Do not tell your child the answer. Write their guess and their reason at the top of the results table. Ask which will sprout first, and which will be tallest, too.

flow.do: 1. Lay the cotton flat on the plate. 2. Pour water over it until it is wet all through, then tip off the extra. 3. Lay 5 moong in a row, then 5 methi, then 5 mustard, a finger-width apart. 4. Put a label at the end of each row.
flow.say: Each kind gets their own row and their own label. Then we can tell them apart later. The cotton must be wet, but with no puddle.
flow.kid: Wet the cotton. Tip off the extra water. Lay five seeds of each kind in a row. Label each row.
flow.parent: Kitchen moong, methi and mustard nearly always sprout. If one kind does not sprout by day 3, the seeds may be old or roasted. Try fresh seeds from a new packet. A puddle can make seeds rot, so keep the cotton wet but not swimming.

flow.do: 1. Put the plate on a window ledge or table in bright light. 2. Keep it out of hot afternoon sun, which can dry the cotton in a few hours.
flow.say: All three rows sit in the same place on the same plate. Why does that matter?
flow.kid: Put the plate by a bright window. Why must all three rows be on one plate?

check.q: Why do all three kinds of seed share one plate of cotton, in one place?
options: So the water, light and warmth are the same, and only the kind of seed is different
So the seeds can help each other grow
check.why: This makes it a fair test. If the seeds grew on different plates, in different places, a difference could come from the water or the light. On one plate, the only difference left is the kind of seed. Picking 'help each other' is a kind thought, but the test is about keeping everything the same.

flow.do: 1. Day 2: add one or two spoons of water if the cotton feels dry. 2. Look for tiny white roots. 3. Write down which seeds have one.
flow.say: Let's see who has woken up. Which seeds have a root?
flow.kid: Is the cotton dry? Add a spoon of water. Which seeds have a tiny white root? Write it down.
flow.parent: The first thing out of a seed is the root. It always grows downwards. Day 3 is the same: a spoon of water, and a quick look for stems standing up.

flow.do: 1. Day 4: look at each row with the magnifying glass. 2. Measure the tallest seedling in each row, from the cotton to the top. 3. Draw one seedling of each kind, showing the shape of the two seed leaves.
flow.say: Look closely at the first two leaves on each seedling. These are called seed leaves. They were folded up inside the seed. Are they the same shape in all three rows?
flow.kid: Look at the first two leaves on each seedling. These are seed leaves. Draw one of each kind. Are they the same shape?
flow.parent: You should see three clear shapes. Moong has a thick stem with the two fat halves of the bean on top, and two small pointed leaves between them. Methi has two small smooth oval leaves. Mustard has two tiny heart-shaped leaves, each with a notch at the top. If the seedlings are still small, wait one more day.

flow.do: Ask your child to compare the five seedlings inside one row, then compare the three rows.
flow.say: Look at the five mustard seedlings. Are they alike? Now look at mustard beside moong. What is the same about all fifteen, and what is different?
flow.kid: Look at the five mustard seedlings. Are they alike? Now look at mustard and moong. What is different?

check.q: All fifteen seeds had the same cotton, water and light. Yet each kind grew their own shape of seed leaf. Where did the shape come from?
options: From the order the seeds were laid down
check.why: Everything outside the seeds was the same for all fifteen. So the only thing that could make the shapes differ is something inside each seed. That is the instructions each seed carries, written in DNA. Picking 'the light' is a fair thought, because light does change how a seedling grows. But all three rows got the same light, so light cannot explain why they differ.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: each kind of seed grows their own shape, because the instructions are inside the seed. What I saw: all fifteen seeds had the same cotton, water and light, but moong, methi and mustard each grew a different shape of seed leaf. The five seedlings of one kind looked alike. Why: each seed carries DNA with the instructions for their own kind. Differences in height inside one row are normal: small things such as the seed's size and position also matter. Keep the seedlings for the Sprout Album project if you like.

experiments.title: Big Seed, Small Seed: does a bigger seed grow a bigger seedling?
experiments.question: Kala chana seeds from one packet come in different sizes. Will the biggest seeds grow taller seedlings than the smallest ones? Will their leaves be a different shape?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After five days, will the seedlings from big seeds be taller, shorter or the same as those from small seeds? Will the leaves be a different shape? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Big and small seeds come from the same packet, so they are the same kind. They grow on the same plate, side by side, with the same water and light. Only the seed size changes. We use 5 of each size, because one seed alone could be a fluke.
results_table: Height of each of the 5 seedlings on day 5 (cm)

materials.item: a handful of whole kala chana (brown chickpeas) from one packet
a bowl of water, for soaking
a steel plate with wet cotton or 4 layers of tissue
a ruler
2 paper labels: BIG and SMALL
a magnifying glass, if you have one

schedule.what: Pick the 5 biggest and the 5 smallest chana. Soak them for about 8 hours, or overnight.
Lay them in two labelled rows on wet cotton by a window.
Add a spoon of water. Look for roots.
Measure all ten seedlings. Add up each row. Compare the leaves.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw one leaf from a big-seed seedling and one from a small-seed seedling, side by side.
experiments.context: In this experiment you test whether big and small seeds of the same kind grow differently. It asks what comes from the instructions, and what comes from the food packed in the seed.

setup.art: A heap of kala chana on a plate, with five big ones and five small ones picked out into two lines.
setup.caption: 1. Pick the 5 biggest and the 5 smallest chana. Soak them overnight.

setup.art: Two labelled rows of soaked chana, BIG and SMALL, on wet cotton in a steel plate by a window.
setup.caption: 2. Lay them in two rows on wet cotton by a window.

setup.art: A child measuring a chana seedling with a ruler, ten seedlings in two rows.
setup.caption: 3. On day 5, measure each seedling and look at the leaves.

flow.do: 1. Pour out a handful of kala chana. 2. Ask your child to pick the 5 biggest and the 5 smallest.
flow.say: All these chana are the same kind, from one packet. Will the big ones grow taller seedlings than the small ones? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pick the five biggest chana and the five smallest. Will the big ones grow taller? Why?

ask.q: Why might a bigger seed grow a bigger seedling?
good: It has more food packed inside.
Any reason is a good start.

flow.parent: Write the guess and reason down. Keep the two groups apart: put the small ones on a paper label marked SMALL.

flow.do: 1. Soak the two groups in two small bowls of water for about 8 hours, or overnight. 2. Next day, lay them in two labelled rows on wet cotton by a window.
flow.say: Soaking wakes the seeds up faster. Both groups get the same soak and the same plate.
flow.kid: Soak the two groups overnight. Next day, lay them in two rows on wet cotton.
flow.parent: Kala chana nearly always sprout within two days. Keep the cotton wet but not swimming, and add a spoon of water each day.

flow.do: Add a spoon of water. Look for roots in both rows.
flow.say: Has every seed got a root? Is one row faster?
flow.kid: Add a spoon of water. Which seeds have a root?

flow.do: 1. Measure each seedling from the cotton to the top of the shoot. 2. Write each height in the table. 3. Add up the 5 heights in each row.
flow.say: Let's measure every one, not just the tallest. Adding up all five gives a fairer picture than one seedling.
flow.kid: Measure every seedling. Write each height. Add up the five in each row.

check.q: The big-seed row adds up to 30 cm. The small-seed row adds up to 20 cm. What does that suggest?
options: Big seeds packed more food, so their seedlings grew faster at first
Small seeds are a different kind of plant
check.why: Both groups are the same kind, from one packet, so they carry the same kind of instructions. A bigger seed has a bigger food store, which feeds the seedling until their leaves can make food from light. Picking 'different instructions' is a fair first thought. But look at the leaves: they are the same shape in both rows. If your results came out the other way, or equal, that is a real result too.

flow.do: 1. Look at the leaves in both rows with the magnifying glass. 2. Then ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Are the leaves a different shape in the two rows? What did size change, and what did it not change?
flow.kid: Look at the leaves in both rows. Same shape or different? What did seed size change?
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: bigger chana seeds grow a little taller at first, but the leaves are the same shape. What I saw: the big-seed row added up to more centimetres, and every leaf was the same small, toothed chana leaf. Why: all the seeds have chana instructions, so they make the same shape. A big seed just has more stored food. Chana leaves open slowly. If you cannot see leaflets yet, wait two more days before comparing the leaves. In many tests the difference in height is small, and some small seeds win. That is fine: it shows other things matter too.

activities.title: Seed Faces: what is hiding in a seed?

materials.item: a few moong, methi and mustard seeds
a white paper and a pencil
a magnifying glass, if you have one

schedule.what: Look closely at three seeds. Draw them. Guess what each plant's leaves will look like.

activities.record: Draw each seed, and beside each one, draw your guess of the leaf that will grow from it.
activities.context: This is a short look-and-wonder activity to start the unit. You study three kitchen seeds and guess what will grow from each.

setup.art: A moong bean, a methi seed and a mustard seed on white paper, seen through a magnifying glass.
setup.caption: 1. Put three seeds on white paper. Look closely.

setup.art: A child's drawing: three seeds on the left, and three guessed leaves with question marks on the right.
setup.caption: 2. Draw each seed, and guess the leaf they will grow.

flow.do: 1. Put one moong, one methi and one mustard seed on white paper. 2. Let your child look with the magnifying glass and draw each one.
flow.say: What do you notice about these three seeds? What do you wonder about them?
flow.kid: Look at the three seeds closely. What do you notice? Draw each one.

good: Methi is yellow and has a corner, with a little groove.
Mustard is round, tiny and dark.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw a guess of the leaf each seed will grow.
flow.say: Each of these seeds can grow into a whole plant. Where is the plant now? Draw the leaf you think each one will grow.
flow.kid: Each seed can grow a whole plant. Where is the plant now? Draw your guess of each leaf.
flow.parent: There is no wrong answer here. Keep the drawings, and compare them with the real seed leaves at the end of the Three Seeds experiment.

activities.title: Same Letters, New Picture: the four-letter code

materials.item: squared paper, or a page with 4 by 4 grids drawn on it
4 colour pencils: red, yellow, blue and green

schedule.what: Colour three 4 by 4 grids from three codes that use the same letters in different orders.

activities.record: Stick the three coloured grids side by side and write the code under each.
activities.context: In this activity you colour pictures from codes made of the four DNA letters. Every code uses the same letters, but in a different order.

setup.art: A key card: A is red, T is yellow, C is blue, G is green, beside three empty 4 by 4 grids.
setup.caption: 1. A is red, T is yellow, C is blue, G is green.

setup.art: Three coloured grids side by side: one with four solid blocks of colour, one with rows of two colours, one with four coloured columns.
setup.caption: 2. Colour each grid from its code, row by row.

flow.do: 1. Write the key at the top of the page: A red, T yellow, C blue, G green. 2. Draw three 4 by 4 grids.
flow.say: DNA has only four letters: A, T, C and G. Today each letter is a colour. Every code fills one grid, row by row, from left to right.
flow.kid: DNA has four letters: A, T, C, G. Here each letter is a colour. Fill each grid row by row.

flow.do: Read out the three codes, one row at a time. Grid 1: AATT, AATT, CCGG, CCGG. Grid 2: ATAT, CGCG, ATAT, CGCG. Grid 3: ACGT, ACGT, ACGT, ACGT.
flow.say: Here is the first code. Row 1 is A, A, T, T. Colour each square as I read it.
flow.kid: Listen to each code. Colour one square for each letter.
flow.parent: Each grid uses four A, four T, four C and four G. Only the order changes. Grid 1 makes four big blocks. Grid 2 makes rows that switch between red and yellow, then blue and green. Grid 3 makes four coloured columns.

flow.do: Lay the three grids side by side and ask the questions.
flow.say: How many red squares are in each grid? So what made the pictures different?
flow.kid: Count the red squares in each grid. Same number? Then why do they look different?

check.q: All three grids use four of each letter. What makes the pictures different?
check.why: Every grid has the same letters, the same number of times. Only the order changes, and the order makes the picture. DNA works the same way: a mustard plant and a person both use A, T, C and G, and the order of the letters makes the difference. Picking 'the number of letters' is a good thing to check, but counting shows it is the same in every grid.

activities.title: The RNA Kitchen: copy one recipe, make one drink

materials.item: a family recipe book or notebook, or a recipe a grown-up writes out on a page
a small slip of paper and a pencil
for neer mor: 1 cup of curd, 3 cups of cold water, a pinch of salt, 6 curry leaves, a small piece of ginger
a jug, a whisk or a spoon, and glasses

activities.safety: A grown-up crushes the ginger. Leave out green chilli for young children.

schedule.what: Copy one recipe from the book onto a slip. Leave the book behind. Make the drink from the slip.

activities.record: Draw a cell as a big circle with a smaller circle inside for the nucleus. Draw the book in the nucleus, the slip on its way out, and the glass of neer mor outside.
activities.context: This activity acts out how a cell uses RNA. The recipe book is the DNA, your slip is the RNA, and the drink is the protein.

setup.art: A recipe notebook open on a bed in another room, a child copying one recipe onto a small slip.
setup.caption: 1. Copy one recipe from the book onto a slip. Leave the book there.

setup.art: The child in the kitchen pouring curd and water into a jug, reading from the slip.
setup.caption: 2. Make the drink from the slip alone.

setup.art: A drawing of a cell: a book in the nucleus, a slip travelling out, a glass of buttermilk beside a small round ribosome.
setup.caption: 3. Draw it as a cell: book, slip and drink.

flow.do: 1. Put the recipe book in a room away from the kitchen. 2. Ask your child to find the neer mor recipe and copy it onto the slip, word by word. 3. The book stays where it is.
flow.say: The book stays in this room, safe from splashes. Copy only the recipe we need onto the slip.
flow.kid: Find the neer mor recipe. Copy it onto your slip. Leave the book here.
flow.parent: If your family has no written recipe, write this on a page first. Neer mor: 1 cup curd, 3 cups cold water, a pinch of salt, 6 curry leaves, a small piece of ginger, crushed. Whisk well.

flow.do: 1. In the kitchen, your child reads the slip and makes the drink. 2. A grown-up crushes the ginger.
flow.say: Read the slip and follow it, one line at a time.
flow.kid: Read your slip. Follow it, one line at a time. Taste it!

flow.do: Ask the questions while you drink, then draw the record together.
flow.say: In a cell, the DNA is like the book. It stays in the nucleus. The cell copies one gene into RNA, like your slip. A tiny part called a ribosome reads the RNA and builds a protein, like your drink. Why do you think the cell copies the gene instead of sending out the DNA?
flow.kid: The book is like DNA. The slip is like RNA. Why copy, and not send the book?

check.q: In a cell, what is like the slip of paper?
check.why: RNA is the copy of one gene, made from the DNA and carried out to be used, just like the slip. The DNA, like the book, stays safe in the nucleus. The protein is what gets built from the copy, like the drink. Picking 'DNA' mixes up the copy with the original.

flow.parent: Good answers: the book stays safe from spills, the cell needs many copies of some recipes at once, and old copies can be thrown away. All of these are true of cells too.

activities.title: Two Metres in a Speck: how much DNA is in one cell?

materials.item: a reel of sewing thread
a measuring tape or a ruler
scissors

schedule.what: Measure 2 metres of thread. Wind it into a small ball. Think about how small a nucleus is.

activities.record: Draw yourself next to a 2-metre line, and next to that a dot for the nucleus.
activities.context: In this activity you measure out as much thread as the DNA in one of your cells would make if it were stretched out.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up stretching a sewing thread along the floor beside a measuring tape that reads 2 metres.
setup.caption: 1. Measure 2 metres of thread along the floor.

setup.art: The thread wound into a small tight ball on a fingertip.
setup.caption: 2. Wind it into a ball as small as you can.

flow.do: 1. Lay the measuring tape on the floor. 2. Unroll thread along it to 2 metres. 3. Cut it.
flow.say: If you stretched out all the DNA in just one of your cells, it would be about this long, 2 metres.
flow.kid: Measure 2 metres of thread. That is the DNA in one of your cells!
flow.parent: 2 metres is taller than most grown-ups. Lie the thread next to a grown-up lying down to compare.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to wind the thread into a ball as small as they can. 2. Then ask the question.
flow.say: A cell folds all this into a nucleus far smaller than the full stop at the end of a sentence. DNA is about a hundred thousand times thinner than this thread. How do you think a cell keeps it from tangling?
flow.kid: Wind it into a tiny ball. Your cells fold DNA much smaller. How do they stop it tangling?
flow.parent: A cell winds DNA around tiny spools made of protein, and then coils the spools up again and again. Each tightly wound piece is a chromosome. Most of your cells have 46. Any thoughtful guess, such as 'wind it round something', is a good answer.

activities.title: Who Gave Me What? A family look-alike hunt

materials.item: family photos, or the family members themselves
a mirror
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Compare your face and hands with family members. Sort your features by where they came from.

activities.record: Make three lists: features that may come from DNA, features from what happened to me, and features from both.
activities.context: In this activity you look for features you share with your family, and sort out which come from DNA and which come from your life.

setup.art: A child holding a mirror beside a framed photo of her mother and grandmother, comparing their noses.
setup.caption: 1. Compare your face with family photos in a mirror.

setup.art: A page with three columns headed DNA, MY LIFE and BOTH, with a few words in each.
setup.caption: 2. Sort your features into three lists.

flow.do: Sit with photos or family members. Look in the mirror together and compare hair, eyes, eyebrows, nose, smile, ears and hands.
flow.say: Which of your features do you see in Amma? In Appa? In a grandparent? Is there anything you have that nobody else has?
flow.kid: Look in the mirror. Then look at your family. Who has your nose? Your smile?
flow.parent: Be gentle in families where a child is adopted or lives with one parent. You can compare with anyone in the home: we all share some features with people we live with, and many with all people.

flow.do: Help your child sort their features into three lists: DNA, my life, and both.
flow.say: Some features come from your DNA. Some come from what happened to you, like a scar or a haircut. Some come from both. Where would you put your height?
flow.kid: Sort your features. DNA, my life, or both? Where does a scar go? Your height?

check.q: Meera, a girl in Class 3, has a small scar on her knee from a fall. Where did the scar come from?
check.why: A scar comes from an injury, not from DNA. A child does not inherit a parent's scar. Height goes in 'both': DNA sets a range, and food and health as a child grow you within it. Picking 'her mother's scar' mixes up features you inherit with things that happen to a body.

projects.title: The Sprout Album: watch the instructions unfold

materials.item: the seedlings from the Three Seeds experiment, or a fresh plate of moong, methi and mustard on wet cotton
a notebook for drawings
a ruler
a small pot or cup of soil from a potted plant, if you have one
a magnifying glass, if you have one

schedule.what: Draw one seedling of each kind. Measure them.
Draw them again. Has anything new appeared?
Move one of each kind into a cup of soil, if you have soil. Draw them.
Draw again. Look for the first true leaves between the seed leaves.
Draw the last page. Lay out all the pages and compare the three kinds.

projects.record: One page per drawing day, with the date, a drawing of each kind and their heights.
projects.context: In this 10-day project you draw the same seedlings again and again, and watch each kind grow their own new leaves.

setup.art: A notebook page with three small seedling drawings labelled moong, methi and mustard, and a date at the top.
setup.caption: 1. Draw one seedling of each kind, with the date.

setup.art: Three paper cups of soil on a window ledge, each with one seedling, labelled.
setup.caption: 2. On day 5, move one of each into soil if you can.

setup.art: Five notebook pages laid out in a row, the seedlings growing taller and new leaves appearing.
setup.caption: 3. On day 10, lay out all your pages.

flow.do: Draw one seedling of each kind, as big as the page allows. Write the date and each height.
flow.say: Each seedling is following their own instructions. Let's draw them every few days and see what they build next.
flow.kid: Draw one of each kind. Write the date. Measure each one.

flow.do: 1. Day 5: fill three cups with soil from a potted plant. 2. Make a hole with a pencil and lower one seedling of each kind in, root first. 3. Water gently.
flow.say: Seedlings on cotton run out of food once their seed is used up. Soil gives them minerals to keep building.
flow.kid: Put each seedling into a cup of soil, root first. Water it gently.
flow.parent: No soil? Keep them on the cotton. They will still grow for a few more days, though more slowly. Soil from a potted plant, or a small bag from any plant nursery, is enough.

flow.do: Draw them again. Look between the seed leaves with the magnifying glass.
flow.say: Look between the seed leaves. Is something new growing there? Does it look like the seed leaves?
flow.kid: Look between the seed leaves. Can you see new leaves? Draw them.
flow.parent: The first true leaves look different from the seed leaves. Methi's true leaves come in threes, like the methi leaves sold in the market. Mustard's are rougher, with wavy edges. Moong's first true leaves are a pair of pointed leaves. Leaves may come a few days late in a cool or dim room.

flow.do: Day 10: lay out all the pages in order and talk about them.
flow.say: Look at all your pages together. Did any seedling ever grow the wrong kind of leaf? What does that tell you?
flow.kid: Lay out all your pages. Did any plant grow the wrong kind of leaf?

check.q: A seedling first opens seed leaves, and later grows true leaves of a different shape. Did the seedling get new instructions?
options: No, the same DNA has the instructions for both, used at different times
check.why: The seedling has the same DNA all along. Their cells use different genes at different stages, first for seed leaves and then for true leaves. Soil and light give the materials and energy, and help the cells decide when to use which genes. Picking 'from the soil' is a common idea, but soil holds no methi instructions: methi and mustard grew different leaves in the same soil.

challenges.title: Code a Kolam: instructions in four letters
challenges.problem: Design a code that uses only the letters A, T, C and G, so that a friend or family member can draw your kolam or pattern exactly, without ever seeing it.
constraints: You may use only the four letters A, T, C and G, written in one long line.
Your partner gets only the code and your key, never the drawing.
Your pattern must have at least 9 dots or squares.
materials: squared paper or a page of dots
general: Give each letter a colour, and fill a grid row by row, as in the four-letter code activity.
Give each letter a direction: A is up, T is down, C is left, G is right. Your partner draws a line one step at a time.
Use pairs of letters: AT means a dot, CG means a gap. More letters per meaning lets you say more things.
creative: Use groups of three letters, like a ribosome does. With four letters there are 64 different groups of three, enough for many shapes and colours.
Add a 'start' group and a 'stop' group, so your partner knows where the pattern begins and ends. Cells use start and stop groups too.
Make one letter change, and see how much your partner's drawing changes.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own code and key. Write out a pattern as a line of letters. Give it to your partner. Compare their drawing with your secret one. What would you change in your code?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You invent a code using only the four DNA letters that lets someone else draw your pattern.

setup.art: A child hiding a drawn kolam behind her back, handing a strip of paper covered in letters A, T, C and G to her brother.
setup.caption: 1. Hide your pattern. Give only the code and key.

setup.art: The brother drawing on dot paper from the strip, the sister comparing his drawing with hers.
setup.caption: 2. Your partner draws it. Compare the two.

flow.do: Your child draws a simple kolam or pattern on squared or dot paper, and hides it.
flow.say: A cell builds a whole body from a line of four letters. Can you write your pattern as a line of four letters?
flow.kid: Draw a small pattern. Hide it. Can you write it with only A, T, C and G?

flow.do: Your child writes a key and a code. A partner draws from them without seeing the pattern.
flow.say: Write a key that says what each letter means. Then write the code. Your partner may not peek.
flow.kid: Write your key. Write your code. Give them to your partner. No peeking!

flow.do: Compare the two drawings and talk about the questions.
flow.say: Do the two drawings match? If not, was it the code or the reading? What would you change?
flow.kid: Do the drawings match? What went wrong? How could your code be clearer?
flow.parent: Mismatches are the best part. They show why a cell needs a clear code that every part reads the same way. Ask: if one letter was copied wrong, how much would the drawing change?
