quiz.p: What are the instructions inside a living thing written in?
quiz.why: Every living thing made of cells keeps their instructions in DNA. Picking 'blood' comes from the old saying 'it runs in the blood', but red blood cells have no DNA.

quiz.p: Moong, methi and mustard seeds grow on the same cotton with the same water and light. What will you see?
opts: All three grow the same leaves
Each kind grows their own shape of leaf
quiz.why: Each seed carries their own instructions, so each kind grows their own shape. Picking 'the same leaves' would mean the cotton and water decide the shape, but they were the same for all.

quiz.p: In a fair test of three kinds of seed, what should be different?
quiz.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the water or place also changed, you could not tell what made the difference.

quiz.p: Which four letters does DNA use?
quiz.why: DNA uses A, T, C and G. These are short names for four chemical parts.

quiz.p: ATG and GTA use the same letters. Why do they mean different things to a cell?
opts: The letters are a different size
The order of the letters is different
quiz.why: In DNA the order of the letters carries the meaning, like 'pat' and 'tap'. Picking 'they mean the same thing' forgets that order matters.

quiz.p: What does RNA do in a cell?
opts: It stores all the instructions for ever
It carries a copy of one gene to where proteins are built
It makes the cell's outer skin
quiz.why: RNA is a working copy of one gene. It leaves the nucleus, and a ribosome reads it to build a protein. The DNA is what stores the instructions.

quiz.p: In a cell, which stays safe in the nucleus, like a recipe book on a shelf?
quiz.why: DNA stays in the nucleus. The cell copies one gene into RNA, like copying one recipe onto a slip.

quiz.p: What do most proteins do in a body?
opts: Most of the work: building, carrying, digesting and protecting
quiz.why: Proteins do most of a body's work. Keratin builds hair, haemoglobin carries oxygen and a protein in spit starts digesting starch.

quiz.p: How much of your DNA came from your mother?
quiz.why: Half of your DNA came from your mother and half from your father. A quarter, roughly, came from each grandparent.

quiz.p: Two brothers, Arun and Vikram, have the same parents but look different. Why?
opts: Each got a different mix of their parents' DNA
quiz.why: Each parent passes on a different mix of genes in every egg or sperm. So brothers and sisters share many features but not all.

quiz.p: Before the 1940s, what did most scientists think carried the instructions?
quiz.why: Most thought DNA, with only four letters, was too simple, and that proteins, with 20 kinds of parts, must carry the instructions. Experiments in 1944 and 1952 showed it was DNA.

quiz.p: In 1952, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase marked a virus's DNA and protein. Which part went inside the bacteria to make new viruses?
quiz.why: Only the DNA went inside the bacteria, and new viruses were built from that DNA. The protein coat stayed outside. This showed that DNA carries the instructions.

items.p: Anjali, a girl in Class 3 in Kochi, grows moong, methi and mustard seeds on one plate of wet cotton. On day 4, each kind has a different shape of seed leaf. What made the shapes different?
items.why: All the seeds shared the same cotton, water and light. Only the seeds were different, so the shapes came from the instructions inside each seed, their DNA. A strong answer says why the other options cannot explain it: they were the same for every seed.

items.p: True or false: a tiny mustard seed carries a full set of mustard instructions.
items.why: True. Even a mustard seed, smaller than a pinhead, has DNA in every one of their cells, with the full instructions for a mustard plant.

items.p: The instructions inside every living thing are written in a molecule called ____.
items.why: DNA is the long, thin molecule that holds a living thing's instructions. It is kept in the nucleus of each cell.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: the long molecule that holds the instructions
one stretch of DNA with instructions for one job
a working copy of one gene
a molecule built from the instructions, which does a job in the body
the part of a cell where the DNA is kept
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These five words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could also give an example of each, such as keratin for a protein.

items.p: How many different letters does DNA use?
items.why: DNA uses four chemical letters: A, T, C and G. With a very long chain of them, four letters are enough to hold all the instructions for a body.

items.p: Sort these into living things that carry DNA and things that do not.
items.a: see items
items.why: Every living thing made of cells carries DNA: birds, trees, insects, bacteria and people. A spoon, a pebble and a bottle are not made of cells, so they have no DNA. A strong answer sorts by whether something is made of cells.

items.p: In the Three Seeds test, why did all fifteen seeds go on one plate, in one place?
items.a: So that the water, light and warmth were the same for every seed. Then the only difference was the kind of seed, and any difference in the seedlings had to come from the seeds.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of a fair test: change only one thing, so you know what caused the result.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show how a cell builds a protein.
items: A ribosome reads the copy and builds the protein
The cell copies one gene into RNA
The DNA sits safe in the nucleus
The RNA copy travels out of the nucleus
a: The DNA sits safe in the nucleus
The cell copies one gene into RNA
The RNA copy travels out of the nucleus
A ribosome reads the copy and builds the protein
items.why: The DNA stays put, a copy is made, the copy leaves the nucleus, and the protein is built from the copy. It is like copying one recipe from a book onto a slip and cooking from the slip.

items.p: Draw the seed leaves of a mustard seedling and a methi seedling, side by side. Label each one.
items.a: Mustard: two tiny heart-shaped leaves, each with a notch at the top. Methi: two small, smooth, oval leaves.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a clear difference in shape, from looking closely at real seedlings.
items.art: Two empty boxes, labelled mustard and methi.

items.p: Karthik says, 'Children get their features from their parents' blood.' True or false?
items.why: False. Features pass on through the DNA in the egg and the sperm. Red blood cells have no DNA at all. The saying 'it runs in the blood' is very old, but it is not how it works.

items.p: Three of these are made by a body, following DNA instructions. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Hair, nails and feathers are built by living cells, mostly from a protein called keratin. A plastic comb is made in a factory and has no DNA instructions behind it.

items.p: Lakshmi has her mother's curly hair and her father's wide smile. Why?
opts: She got half her DNA from each parent
She ate the same food as them
She looked at them every day
items.why: A child inherits half of their DNA from the mother and half from the father, so they can have features from each. Copying or looking cannot change hair or a smile.

items.p: A cell copies one gene into a shorter molecule called ____.
items.why: RNA is the working copy of one gene. It is carried out of the nucleus and read to build a protein.

items.p: Two friends in Chennai look at a plate of seedlings. Moong, methi and mustard grew side by side on the same cotton.

views.says: The seedlings are different because the seeds are different. Each seed carries their own instructions.
The cotton, water and light matter most. Without them, no seed would grow at all.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with more? Use what you saw in the Three Seeds test. Then say what the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both are right about different things. The shape came from inside each seed, because everything outside was the same, so Divya explains why they differ. Farhan is right that water, light and warmth give the materials and energy: a dry seed never sprouts.
items.why: Instructions and surroundings both shape a living thing. A strong answer uses the test to show which one explains the difference here.

items.p: Where in a cell is the DNA kept?
opts: On the outside of the cell
In the blood around the cell
items.why: DNA is kept in the nucleus, a round part of the cell. Your red blood cells are the exception: they lose their nucleus as they grow, so they carry no DNA.

items.p: Your family's recipe book stays on a shelf, and you cook from a copy on a slip. Which part of a cell is like the book, and which is like the slip? Why does a cell use a copy?
items.a: The DNA is like the book, kept safe in the nucleus. The RNA is like the slip, a copy of one gene. The cell uses a copy so that the DNA stays safe, and so it can make many copies of a gene when it needs a lot of one protein.
items.why: A strong answer names both parts correctly and gives at least one reason for copying.

items.p: Kala chana from one packet were sorted into big and small seeds and grown side by side. What would you expect on day 5?
opts: The big seeds grow a different kind of leaf
The big seeds often grow a little taller, with the same shape of leaf
The small seeds grow into a different plant
items.why: Big and small chana carry the same kind of instructions, so the leaves have the same shape. A bigger seed packs more food, which can help the seedling grow faster at first. A strong answer separates what the instructions decide from what the food store changes.

items.p: The same moong seeds grow tall and pale in the dark, and short and green in the light. Does that mean DNA does not matter? Explain.
items.a: No. The DNA still makes them moong: they have moong leaves and moong stems in both places. The light changes how the cells use their genes, so the same instructions give a different height and colour. Both DNA and surroundings matter.
items.why: A strong answer shows that surroundings change how instructions are used, not which kind of plant grows.

items.p: True or false: a skin cell and a bone cell in your body carry different DNA.
items.why: False. Almost every cell in your body has the same DNA. A skin cell and a bone cell use different genes from it, like cooks using different pages of one cookbook.

items.p: In RNA, which letter is used in place of T?
items.why: RNA uses U in place of T. Otherwise the copy says the same thing as the gene it came from.

items.p: With only four letters, how can DNA hold enough instructions for a whole tree? Give an example with letters.
items.a: Because the order of the letters matters, and the chain is very long. ATG and GTA use the same letters but mean different things. One set of human DNA has about 3 billion letter pairs, so there are endless possible orders.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that order, not the number of kinds of letter, carries the meaning, and gives a short example.

items.p: Put these in order, from biggest to smallest.
items.why: Your body is made of cells. Inside each cell is a nucleus. Inside the nucleus is the DNA, and a gene is one short stretch of it.

items.p: Sort these features of Priya, a girl in Class 4. Did each one come from her DNA, from her life, or both?
items.a: see items
items.why: Blood group and ear shape come almost entirely from DNA. A scar and a haircut come from what happened to her. Height and strong arms come from DNA and from food and exercise. A strong answer gives a reason for each 'both'.

items.p: Match each protein to its job.
pairs: helps the body use sugar from food
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Every one of these proteins is built from instructions in a gene. A strong answer can say one way each protein helps the body.

items.p: A family in Mysuru argues about where a baby's looks come from.

views.says: She has her mother's eyes. It runs in the blood.
Her eyes came from DNA, half from me and half from her father. Blood has nothing to do with it.
She looks like nobody. She looks like herself.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Use what you learned about DNA. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Revathi that looks pass on through DNA, not blood. It gives Paati her due: families really do share features, which is what she noticed. And Arjun is right too: each child gets a new mix of their parents' DNA, so no one else looks exactly like them.
items.why: Each view sees something true. A strong answer uses the facts about DNA and is fair to every view.

items.p: A ribosome reads RNA in groups of how many letters?
items.why: A ribosome reads three letters at a time. Each group of three tells it which amino acid to add next, or to stop.

items.p: Draw a cell as a big circle with a nucleus inside. Draw the DNA in the nucleus, an RNA copy leaving it, and a ribosome building a protein. Label all four.
items.a: A big circle with a smaller circle inside. In the small circle, a long twisted line labelled DNA. A short line labelled RNA crossing out of the nucleus. A small round ribosome with a chain of beads, labelled protein.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the DNA staying inside and the copy going out, in the right order.

items.p: Most of your cells have 46 chromosomes: ____ from your mother and ____ from your father.
items.why: 46 shared equally between two parents is 23 each. That is why a child gets half of their DNA from each parent.

items.p: A seedling opens seed leaves first, and later grows true leaves of a new shape. Where did the instructions for the true leaves come from?
items.a: From the same DNA the seedling had all along. The cells use different genes at different times, first for seed leaves and then for true leaves.
items.why: A strong answer says no new instructions arrive: the plant uses different parts of the same DNA as they grow.

items.p: Identical twins grow from one fertilised egg that split in two. What is true about their DNA?
opts: It changes to match their friends
items.why: Identical twins share the same DNA, because they came from one egg. They still have different fingerprints and grow up a little different, because surroundings shape bodies too.

items.p: Your red blood cells have no nucleus, and so no DNA. Use this to explain why a blood transfusion does not change how a person looks.
items.a: The blood a person receives is mostly red blood cells, which carry no DNA. And looks are built by the DNA in a person's own cells, from before they were born. So new blood cannot give anyone new instructions for their looks.
items.why: A strong answer joins two facts: red blood cells lack DNA, and looks come from the body's own DNA.

items.p: Design a test to show that the shape of a methi leaf comes from the methi seed, not from the soil. Say what you would keep the same and what you would change.
items.a: Grow methi seeds and mustard seeds in the same soil, in the same pot, with the same water and light. Then also grow methi seeds in two different soils. If methi always grows methi leaves in both soils, and mustard grows mustard leaves in the same soil as methi, the shape comes from the seed.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing at a time: the kind of seed, or the soil, and keeps everything else the same.

items.p: Scientists put the human gene for insulin into bacteria, and the bacteria made human insulin. What does this show?
opts: Bacteria and people read DNA in almost the same way
Genes only work in the body they came from
items.why: The bacteria read a human gene correctly and built the human protein. That works only because almost all living things use the same four letters and nearly the same code. Since the 1980s, insulin for people with diabetes has been made this way.

items.p: In the early 1940s, two scientists argue about what carries a living thing's instructions.

views.says: Proteins carry the instructions. They are made of 20 kinds of parts. DNA has only four, so it is too simple.
When I destroyed the protein, bacteria still changed. When I destroyed the DNA, they did not. So DNA carries the instructions.

items.ask: Which scientist would you have believed in 1944? What evidence would have changed your mind? Then say why the protein scientist's idea made sense at the time.
items.a: A strong answer sides with Avery because of the test: removing DNA stopped the change, removing protein did not. Hershey and Chase's 1952 virus test added more evidence. It is fair to the protein scientist: 20 kinds of parts did seem able to say more, and nobody yet knew how long DNA was.
items.why: The protein idea was reasonable but wrong. A strong answer shows how evidence, not how complicated something looks, settled it.

items.p: A cell in a mustard leaf and a cell in the same plant's root have the same DNA. Explain how they can do such different jobs.
items.a: Each cell uses different genes from the same DNA. The leaf cell uses the genes for chlorophyll and catching light. The root cell uses genes for taking in water. The cells sense where they are, such as light or dark, and switch genes on or off.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of the same book with different pages read, and says something about how a cell senses where they are.

items.p: Draw a twisted ladder of DNA with 6 rungs. Write a letter on each end of every rung. Remember: A always pairs with T, and C with G.
items.a: Six rungs, each with one of the pairs A and T, T and A, C and G, or G and C. For example A-T, C-G, G-C, T-A, A-T, G-C.
items.why: A strong drawing never pairs A with C or G, or T with C or G. The pairing rule is how a cell can copy DNA exactly.
items.art: Two long wavy lines twisting around each other, with six empty rungs.

items.p: An onion cell holds about five times as much DNA as a human cell. What does this tell us?
opts: Onions are five times cleverer than people
The amount of DNA does not tell you how complicated a living thing is
Human cells have lost their DNA
items.why: Many plants have far more DNA than people, much of it repeated many times. So more DNA does not mean a bigger or more complicated body. A strong answer avoids ranking living things by their DNA.

items.p: Two sisters have the same mother and father. Why can they still look different from each other?
items.a: Each parent has two sets of DNA, and passes on a different mix of it in every egg or sperm. So each sister gets her own mix of half her mother's and half her father's DNA. Their different lives also shape them.
items.why: A strong answer explains that each child gets a different mix, and mentions surroundings too.

items.p: True or false: every virus keeps their genes in DNA.
items.why: False. Many viruses, such as the flu virus and the virus that causes COVID-19, keep their genes in RNA. Living things made of cells all keep their instructions in DNA.

items.p: Sort each statement into the kind of statement it is.
items: DNA carries the instructions passed from parents to young
A ribosome reads RNA three letters at a time
How life first began, and whether RNA came first
How all of a cell's choices about genes fit together
A child gets half of their DNA from each parent
items.a: see items
items.why: Good science keeps what is shown apart from what is still open. A strong answer gives a reason, such as the experiment behind each settled one.

items.p: If you read one DNA letter every second, day and night, one set of your DNA would take nearly 100 years. Why might it matter that a cell can copy all of it, many times, without mistakes?
items.a: Every time a cell splits, each new cell needs a full, correct copy of the instructions. If the copy had many mistakes, the new cells might build the wrong proteins and not work well.
items.why: A strong answer joins the size of the DNA to the need for careful copying when cells divide.

items.p: Which of these does NOT keep their instructions in DNA?
items.why: The mango tree, the curd bacterium and the elephant are all made of cells, and all keep their instructions in DNA. The flu virus keeps their genes in RNA.

items.p: Martha Chase did the 1952 experiment with Alfred Hershey, but only Hershey shared the Nobel Prize. Why do you think this happened, and why does it matter to say her name?
items.a: She was a young assistant, and prizes usually went to the senior scientist, and at that time women's work was often left out. Saying her name matters because she did the work, and children should know that women make discoveries too.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason from history and says something fair about credit for shared work.

items.p: Venki Ramakrishnan, born in Chidambaram in Tamil Nadu, won a Nobel Prize in 2009 for working out the structure of a ribosome. Why is the ribosome so important?
opts: It reads RNA and builds proteins
It makes the cell's outer skin
It carries oxygen in the blood
items.why: Ribosomes are the parts of a cell that read RNA copies and join amino acids into proteins. Every cell in every living thing has them. Knowing their shape helped scientists understand how many medicines that fight bacteria work.

items.p: In DNA, A always pairs with ____, and C always pairs with ____.
items.why: These pairs are always the same. That is how one strand of the ladder can be used to build the other when DNA is copied.

items.p: Some people say 'my genes made me do it.' Using what you know about DNA and surroundings, explain why this is only partly true.
items.a: Genes shape a body and some of how it works. But surroundings, choices and what happens to us also shape us, as the moong in the dark and the twins' fingerprints show. So genes are part of the story, not all of it.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence from the unit on both sides and says neither one alone explains a living thing.

applications: Doctors read a patient's DNA to find the cause of some rare illnesses.
Bacteria given the human gene for insulin make insulin for people with diabetes.
DNA tests can show who is related to whom, and help police solve crimes.
Farmers and scientists breed new rice and millet varieties by choosing plants with useful genes.
Some vaccines, such as several COVID-19 vaccines, give the body an RNA copy of one virus gene, so the immune system learns to fight the virus.
Scientists read DNA from water and soil to find out which animals live in a lake or forest without seeing them.
Wildlife scientists in India test DNA from seized skins and ivory, to find which kind of animal they came from, and sometimes from which region.

open_questions.q: How did the first instructions for life begin?
open_questions.why_open: Many scientists think life began with RNA, which can carry instructions and do some jobs too. Nobody has yet made RNA that fully copies itself, so the idea is still being tested.

open_questions.q: How does a cell decide, moment by moment, which genes to use?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know many of the molecules that switch genes on and off, but not yet how all of a cell's choices fit together.

open_questions.q: What does most of our DNA do?
open_questions.why_open: Only a small part of human DNA holds the instructions for proteins. Some of the rest helps switch genes on and off. What much of it does is still argued about.

open_questions.q: Why do some plants, such as onions, have far more DNA than people?
open_questions.why_open: Much of it is repeated many times. Why some living things keep so much extra DNA is not fully understood.

open_questions.q: How exactly does a body follow DNA to grow the right shape, such as a leaf in threes or a hand with five fingers?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know many of the genes involved, but how cells work together to make a whole shape is still being studied.

ask_kids: Which of your features do you think came from Amma? Which from Appa?
This dosa batter was rice and urad dal. Where were their instructions?
If every cell in you has the same DNA, how does your eye know to be an eye?
A neem seed and a mango stone can land on the same soil. Why do they grow differently?
What would happen if a recipe was copied with one word wrong?
Is there anything about you that is not in your DNA?
Why do you think the cell copies a gene, instead of sending out the DNA itself?
The crow at the window had a mother and father crow. What did they pass on?

jokes.j: What did the DNA say to the other DNA?
jokes.a: Do these genes make me look twisted?

jokes.j: Why did the mustard seed never become a mango tree?
Why was the RNA always in a hurry?
jokes.a: It had a message to deliver.

jokes.j: What do you call a gene that tells jokes?
Why did the cell keep their DNA in the nucleus?
jokes.a: Because it was too precious to leave lying around the kitchen.

jokes.j: Why did the moong sprout feel proud?
jokes.a: They followed every instruction to the letter.

jokes.j: What did the methi seedling say to the mustard seedling?
jokes.a: We grew up in the same place, but you're just not my type.

jokes.j: Why did Paati's cookbook never go into the kitchen?
jokes.a: It didn't want to get into a sticky situation, just like DNA.

maths.problem: DNA has four letters: A, T, C and G. How many different two-letter codes can you make, such as AT, TA or GG?
maths.explain: The first letter can be any of 4. For each first letter, the second can be any of 4. So there are 4 groups of 4. 4 times 4 is 16. You can check by listing them: AA, AT, AC, AG, then TA, TT, TC, TG, and so on.
maths.context: This is about the four-letter code activity, where each DNA letter stood for a colour.
maths.why_maths: Counting the possible codes shows why four letters are enough: every extra letter in a group multiplies the number of things a code can say.

maths.problem: A ribosome reads RNA in groups of three letters. With four letters, there are 64 different groups of three. Cells use about 20 amino acids. Are there enough groups for every amino acid to have at least one?
maths.explain: 64 groups and 20 amino acids. 64 take away 20 is 44. So every amino acid can have a group, and 44 groups are left over. Cells use some of the extra groups as 'stop' signs, and many amino acids have more than one group.
maths.context: This is about how a ribosome reads RNA three letters at a time, to choose each amino acid in a protein.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two numbers tells us whether the code could work. Two-letter groups would give only 16, which is not enough for 20 amino acids.

maths.problem: Most of your cells have 46 chromosomes, half from each parent. How many came from your father?
maths.explain: Half of 46 means 46 shared into 2 equal groups. 46 divided by 2 is 23. Check: 23 + 23 = 46.
maths.context: This is about chromosomes, the tightly wound pieces of DNA in each cell.
maths.why_maths: Halving shows exactly how a child's DNA is shared between the two parents.

maths.problem: In the Big Seed, Small Seed test, the five big-seed seedlings measured 7, 6, 6, 5 and 6 cm. The five small-seed seedlings measured 5, 4, 3, 4 and 4 cm. Add up each row. Which row grew more, and by how much?
maths.answer: Big seeds: 30 cm. Small seeds: 20 cm. The big-seed row grew 10 cm more.
maths.explain: Big: 7 + 6 + 6 + 5 + 6 = 30. Small: 5 + 4 + 3 + 4 + 4 = 20. 30 take away 20 is 10. Notice that the shortest big-seed seedling, 5 cm, was as tall as the tallest small-seed seedling. That is why we measure five, not one.
maths.context: This is about the Big Seed, Small Seed experiment. You grew the five biggest and five smallest kala chana from one packet side by side. These are made-up example results.

chart.title: Total height of five seedlings (made-up results)

maths.why_maths: Adding all five heights is fairer than comparing one seedling from each row, because one seedling can be a fluke.

maths.problem: The DNA in one of your cells would be about 2 metres long if stretched out. How many centimetres is that? If you laid the DNA from 5 cells end to end, how long would it be?

roots.context: We have grown three kinds of seed side by side, and learned that each carries their own instructions in DNA. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your moong, methi and mustard seeds sprouted on the same wet cotton, by the same window. Each still grew their own shape of seed leaf. The water, light and cotton were the same for all three. So each shape came from instructions carried inside the seeds.
deep_truth.habit: We often say soil, water and sun make a plant. They give the materials and the energy, but they gave all three seeds the same things. The plan for each plant's shape travelled inside the seed.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Three Seeds test, fifteen seeds shared one plate, one water and one window. Moong grew fat bean halves, methi grew small oval seed leaves and mustard grew notched heart-shaped ones, and the five seedlings of each kind looked alike.

three.who_am_i: Every cell of you carries the same DNA, half from your mother and half from your father. That plan was copied, without a break, from parents long before them.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing made of cells carries their own instructions, and uses them to build their own body from water, air and food.
three.what_is_this_world: A mustard plant, a crow and you all write your instructions in the same four letters, A, T, C and G.

roots.thread: DNA uses only four letters, yet every kind of living thing is written in them: a mustard plant, a neem tree, an ant, a crow and you. One code, in countless orders, gives countless bodies. And because every living thing with cells uses this same code, scientists think all of them came from one shared ancestor, long ago. So the many kinds of life are one family, written in one script.

science.text: All known living things with cells keep their instructions in DNA, with the same four letters and almost the same code. This is strong evidence that all of them share one ancestor.
How a cell weighs everything they sense to choose which genes to use is still being worked out.

other_view.view: Calling DNA 'instructions' or a 'code' is a helpful comparison, but no one wrote the code and nothing reads it the way a person reads a book. It is chemistry: molecules fitting together. Reading meaning into it says more about us than about DNA.

practice.title: Hold a seed
practice.say: Let's each hold one mustard seed in our palm. Look at how small it is. Now close your eyes and breathe slowly, five times. Inside this seed is the plan for a whole mustard plant, with yellow flowers. Inside your own body, every cell holds a plan too. Some of it came from your grandmother, and from her grandmother. Open your eyes. Look at the seed again.
practice.kid: Hold one mustard seed. Look how small it is. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly five times. A whole plant's plan is inside. Your cells hold a plan too. Open your eyes.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, with the materials listed. Kitchen moong, methi and mustard almost always sprout on wet cotton within two days in Indian room temperatures. Their seed leaves are clearly different by day 4: fat moong halves, small oval methi leaves and tiny notched mustard leaves. Roasted or very old seeds will not sprout, so the steps say to try a fresh packet. A puddle of water rots seeds, so the steps say wet but not swimming. Hot afternoon sun can dry cotton in hours, so the plate sits in bright light but out of direct afternoon sun. Kala chana from one packet vary enough in size to pick clear big and small groups, and sprout after an overnight soak. Chana leaves open slowly, so the step says to wait two more days if needed. The RNA Kitchen uses curd, water, salt, curry leaves and ginger, and a grown-up crushes the ginger. Green chilli is left out for young children. The look-alike hunt has a note for adoptive and single-parent families. Both games work for one child alone and need only paper and a pencil. The spine (intro, Seed Faces, Three Seeds, explanations, roots, quiz) fits about 85 minutes over two sessions, with short checks on days 2 and 3.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1869 Friedrich Miescher, a young Swiss doctor working in Tübingen, Germany, washed white blood cells off used hospital bandages. From the nucleus of these cells he got a new substance, which he called nuclein. Today we call it DNA. For the next 70 years, most scientists thought nuclein was too simple to matter. The chemist Phoebus Levene showed it was made of only four kinds of small parts, and many took this to mean it was a dull, repeating chain. Proteins, with 20 kinds of parts, seemed far better for holding instructions. In 1944, Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty in New York gave harmless bacteria a liquid from dead, harmful ones. The harmless bacteria became harmful. When they destroyed the protein in the liquid, it still worked. When they destroyed the DNA, it stopped. Many scientists still doubted. Then in 1952, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase, his 24-year-old assistant, marked the DNA and the protein of a virus with different radioactive atoms. Only the DNA went inside the bacteria the virus attacked, and new viruses were built from that DNA. DNA carried the instructions. Hershey later shared a Nobel Prize. Chase did not.
how_we_found_out.who: Friedrich Miescher, Phoebus Levene, Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, Maclyn McCarty, Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: For about 70 years most scientists thought DNA, with only four letters, was too simple to carry instructions, and that proteins must carry them. Avery's bacteria and Hershey and Chase's viruses showed that DNA, not protein, passes the instructions on.
